# The Future of Project Management in Canada: Connecting Delivery, Business Needs, and Data

Project management in Canada is likely to become more focused on technology, business value, and evidence. Managing scope, schedule, and cost will remain essential. However, project professionals will also need to understand business requirements, interpret data, and help people adopt change.

Canadian evidence supports this direction. Artificial intelligence adoption is increasing, government systems need modernization, and federal digital standards encourage continuous improvement. These developments bring project management, business analysis, and data analytics closer together.

## What the Canadian data tells us

Statistics Canada reports the following adoption rates for businesses using artificial intelligence to produce goods or deliver services during the previous 12 months:

| Survey period | Businesses reporting AI use |
|---|---:|
| Second quarter of 2024 | 6.1% |
| Second quarter of 2025 | 12.2% |
| Second quarter of 2026 | 19.2% |

Source: Statistics Canada, *Analysis on artificial intelligence use by businesses in Canada, second quarter of 2026*.

Using these figures, adoption increased by **7.0 percentage points** from 2025 to 2026. The relative increase was approximately **57.4%**, calculated as `(19.2 − 12.2) ÷ 12.2 × 100`.

This is **descriptive analysis**: it explains what changed. It does not prove that AI caused better project performance or increased project management employment. These are business adoption figures, rather than a survey of project managers.

The practical implication is that more projects may involve AI selection, implementation, training, and evaluation. Project managers will need to turn these activities into clear deliverables and measurable outcomes.

## AI will change project tasks and decisions

A reasonable expectation is that AI will assist with drafting status reports, summarizing meetings, identifying patterns, and preparing initial risk assessments. These are possible applications, rather than guaranteed results.

For a PMP professional, AI output still needs to be checked against the **scope baseline**, **schedule baseline**, **risk register**, and approved decisions. A suggested deadline is useful only when it reflects real dependencies and available resources.

For a business analyst, an AI-generated requirement should be validated through **requirements elicitation**, stakeholder review, and clear **acceptance criteria**.

The important capability will be knowing when information is reliable enough to support a decision.

## Government modernization will require stronger governance

The Auditor General’s 2023 audit reported that approximately two-thirds of federal applications were in poor health and needed modernization. It also identified approximately 2,100 active IT projects with total planned costs of about $44 billion. These are historical audit findings, not a count of today’s projects.

This evidence shows the scale and complexity of public-sector technology delivery. Replacing an old system can involve data migration, procurement, integration, training, and service continuity.

In PMP terminology, this requires **risk management**, **stakeholder engagement**, **change control**, and clear **governance**—who makes decisions and who is accountable.

More recently, the federal government announced Digital Transformation Canada on September 3, 2026. Its stated priorities include shared solutions, reduced duplication, modern tools, and more strategic technology procurement. This is evidence of policy direction; successful delivery still needs to be demonstrated.

## Delivery approaches will need to fit the project

Canada’s federal Digital Standards encourage designing with users, improving services frequently, protecting privacy, and being responsible data stewards.

These principles support iterative delivery. However, projects may also require fixed budgets, formal approvals, and contractual milestones.

A **hybrid approach** can combine predictive planning with Agile development. For example, a team could establish funding and procurement milestones while delivering software through short sprints.

PMI’s global research reported that hybrid approach use increased from 20% in 2020 to 31.5% in 2023. This supports the wider trend toward flexible delivery, although it is not a Canadian adoption statistic.

## Business analysis will connect delivery to value

A project can deliver its agreed scope while failing to solve the original problem. Strong business analysis helps prevent this.

A business analyst examines the **current state**, defines the **future state**, and performs **gap analysis**. Requirements traceability connects the business need to requirements, deliverables, and testing.

Consider a hypothetical online application project. Launching the portal is an **output**. Reducing processing time is an **outcome**. Lower operating costs and easier access are potential **benefits**.

A clear business case should identify these benefits, their owners, and how they will be measured after implementation. This makes **benefits realization** part of project success.

## Data analytics will make reporting more useful

Project reporting should help leaders decide what to do next.

| Analysis type | Question | Project example |
|---|---|---|
| Descriptive | What happened? | Report milestone delays |
| Diagnostic | Why did it happen? | Investigate approval bottlenecks |
| Predictive | What might happen? | Forecast completion dates |
| Prescriptive | What should we do? | Compare recovery options |

A useful dashboard could combine delivery indicators, such as **Cost Performance Index (CPI)** and **Schedule Performance Index (SPI)** where earned value management is appropriate, with business **KPIs**, such as processing time, adoption rate, and error rate.

Data quality matters. Teams need consistent definitions, reliable baselines, and clear reporting periods. A dashboard cannot correct inaccurate source data.

## What this means for Canadian project professionals

PMI’s 2025 talent-gap report projects North American demand growth of approximately 21%–26% for project professionals between 2025 and 2035. This is a regional forecast, not a Canadian job guarantee.

The evidence suggests that Canadian professionals should develop three connected capabilities: disciplined project delivery, strong business analysis, and confident use of data.

PMP knowledge provides structure. Business analysis clarifies what matters. Data analytics helps show whether the change worked. Communication, judgment, and stakeholder engagement connect all three.

## References

1. Statistics Canada. (2026). [*Analysis on artificial intelligence use by businesses in Canada, second quarter of 2026*](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-621-m/11-621-m2026010-eng.htm).
2. Office of the Auditor General of Canada. (2023). [*Report 7—Modernizing Information Technology Systems*](https://www.canada.ca/en/auditor-general/our-work/audit-reports/parl-oag-202310-07-e.html).
3. Prime Minister of Canada. (2026, September 3). [*Launch of Digital Transformation Canada*](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2026/09/03/prime-minister-carney-launches-digital-transformation-canada-deliver).
4. Government of Canada. [*Digital Standards Playbook*](https://www.canada.ca/en/government/system/digital-government/government-canada-digital-standards.html).
5. Project Management Institute. (2024). [*Pulse of the Profession*](https://www.pmi.org/-/media/pmi/documents/public/pdf/learning/thought-leadership/pmi-pulse-of-the-profession-2024-report.pdf).
6. Project Management Institute. (2025). [*Global Project Management Talent Gap*](https://www.pmi.org/-/media/pmi/documents/public/pdf/learning/thought-leadership/talent_gap_2025-v3.pdf)
